docs.title: v3.0
docs.text:
PicoKey App 3.0 adds:

  • a dedicated FIDO > Vault panel for local opaque credential packages;
  • export and import of selected resident credentials through an enrolled Pico Vault;
  • four Vault encryption profile choices;
  • Vault metadata such as RP, user, algorithm, board serial, and Vault ID;
  • Vault groups packages from multiple Vault IDs and permits import only when the board's active Vault ID matches;
  • bulk Vault import/export and per-credential Vault actions;
  • per-credential expiration and revocation actions;
  • PIN complexity policy configuration;
  • alwaysUv, makeCredUvNotRqd, and discoverable-credential controls;
  • a FIDO Dashboard switch for the Keyboard Interface used by OTP slots 1 to 4;
  • better FIDO transport fallback when the HID path is unavailable; and
  • improved OpenPGP/PIV panel behavior for mixed FIDO2 devices.

Use the standalone Pico Vault Enroller to enroll a board. After enrollment, PicoKey App manages exported packages but does not perform the enrollment ceremony.

docs.title: Security initialization
docs.text:
Use PicoKey App to configure these security initialization and provisioning options.

These options are applied during initialization and shape the device's security model.

docs.title: Secure Boot
docs.text:
When enabled:

  • Firmware authenticity is verified at boot
  • Only signed firmware images are allowed

Note

Secure Boot is strongly recommended for production devices.

docs.title: Secure Lock
docs.text:
Locks the boot keys permanently.

  • Prevents boot key replacement
  • Protects against firmware downgrade attacks

Danger

Secure Lock is irreversible. Enabling it incorrectly may permanently brick the device.

docs.title: Applying security options
docs.text: After choosing the settings, click Enable Security Options to apply them to the device.

docs.title: Registration requirement
docs.text: Register the board in PicoKey App before applying security settings from this panel.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Use this guide to check common PicoKey App problems before opening a support ticket.

docs.title: Device not detected
docs.text: PicoKey App does not detect the connected device.

docs.title: Possible causes
docs.text:
• The device is not connected correctly
  • The USB cable does not support data
  • Another application is accessing the device
  • USB permissions are missing (Linux)
  • The device is in an unexpected mode

docs.title: Recommended actions
docs.text:
• Use a direct USB port on the computer (avoid hubs)
  • Try a different USB cable
  • Close other applications that may access USB devices
  • Disconnect and reconnect the device
  • Restart PicoKey App

Tip

For first-time setup, always use a direct USB connection without hubs.

docs.title: Device detected but in unexpected connection mode
docs.text: The device is detected, but the Connection field shows an unexpected value.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
The connection mode depends on the firmware and device state.

Common modes include:

  • RESCUE (BOOTSEL / recovery mode)
  • Normal operation mode (firmware-dependent)

docs.title: What to do
docs.text:
• A new or freshly flashed device is expected to be in RESCUE mode.
  • If the device should be in normal mode, reconnect it and check again.
  • If you are unsure, commission the device only when instructed.

Note

Connection mode alone does not indicate a faulty device.

docs.title: License installed but board is not registered
docs.text: A license is installed, but the board status remains Not registered.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text: Installing a license and registering a board are separate steps. Install the license first, then bind it to the selected board.

docs.title: Recommended actions
docs.text:
• Go to About → License
  • Verify that the license is correctly installed
  • Select the correct board type
  • Click Register Board

Warning

Board registration is a required step and cannot be skipped.

docs.title: Selected the wrong board type
docs.text: The wrong board type was selected during registration.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
Board type selection is user-controlled and irreversible. Once the board is registered, you cannot change the selected type.

Danger

Selecting an incorrect board type cannot be undone.

The license will remain bound to the selected board type permanently.

docs.title: What to do
docs.text:
• Do not select a similar board as a workaround.
  • Do not try to register the board again.

Instead, open a support ticket and explain the situation.

docs.title: My board does not appear in the board list
docs.text: The board selection list does not include your board model.

docs.title: Recommended actions
docs.text:
• Do not proceed with board registration
  • Do not select a different or similar board

Danger

Registering a board with an incorrect board type may permanently bind the license incorrectly.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
Open a ticket at:

https://github.com/polhenarejos/picokeyapp/issues

Include:

  • The exact board model
  • PicoKey App version
  • Firmware version
  • Any relevant screenshots or logs

docs.title: Firmware update fails
docs.text: The firmware update does not complete successfully.

docs.title: Possible causes
docs.text:
• USB connection interrupted
  • Device disconnected during update
  • Incorrect firmware file
  • Device not in the expected mode

docs.title: Recommended actions
docs.text:
• Do not unplug the device immediately
  • Follow any instructions shown by PicoKey App
  • If the device reappears in RESCUE mode, retry the update
  • Use a direct USB connection

Warning

Interrupting a firmware update may require recovery steps.

docs.title: Features missing after firmware update
docs.text: Some features are missing after installing or updating firmware.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
Available features depend on the installed firmware rather than PicoKey App.

Installing another firmware variant may:

  • Enable new features
  • Disable features available in a previous firmware
  • Require re-commissioning

docs.title: Recommended actions
docs.text:
• Verify the installed firmware version
  • Review the documentation for the selected firmware variant
  • Re-run commissioning if required

Note

PicoKey App only exposes features supported by the firmware.

docs.title: Permission issues (Linux)
docs.text: The device is detected, but operations fail on Linux.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text: Linux may require additional USB permissions before the device can be used.

docs.title: Recommended actions
docs.text:
• Check udev rules
  • Ensure the user belongs to the appropriate groups
  • Restart the session after changing permissions

Tip

Running PicoKey App from a terminal can help identify permission-related errors.

docs.title: When to open a support ticket
docs.text:
Open a support ticket when:

  • The correct board model is not listed
  • Firmware recovery is not possible
  • The device behaves inconsistently after following this guide

Use the official issue tracker:

https://github.com/polhenarejos/picokeyapp/issues

Include the details above so the support team can investigate the issue.

docs.title: Accounts
docs.text: Use the Accounts panel to manage OATH accounts stored on the device.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The panel lets you:

  • list existing accounts;
  • add TOTP and HOTP accounts;
  • rename or delete accounts; and
  • review account status before provisioning.

docs.title: Access control (OATH password)
docs.text:
You can protect the OATH applet with an access password. Depending on the device state, the panel offers:

  • Set Access: define an OATH access password
  • Unlock: unlock the OATH session
  • Change Access: rotate the OATH access password
  • Clear Access: remove the OATH access password

When the applet is locked, account details remain hidden until you unlock it.

docs.title: Add TOTP
docs.text: Use the TOTP form to add an entry that generates time-based codes.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• Name: account label in the format issuer:account.
  • Secret: Shared OATH secret used to generate codes.
  • Type: Time based (TOTP).
  • Algorithm: hash algorithm (SHA1, SHA256, SHA512).
  • Period: Time step in seconds for code rotation (commonly 30).
  • Digits: OTP output length (typically 6 or 8).
  • Require touch: requires user touch/presence for code use.

Note

Exact field names can vary slightly depending on firmware and app version.

docs.title: Add HOTP
docs.text: Use the HOTP form to add an entry that generates counter-based codes.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• Name: account label in the format issuer:account.
  • Secret: Shared OATH secret used to generate codes.
  • Type: Counter based (HOTP).
  • Algorithm: hash algorithm (SHA1, SHA256, SHA512).
  • Counter: Initial counter value used for the first HOTP code.
  • Digits: OTP output length (typically 6 or 8).
  • Require touch: requires user touch/presence for code use.

Note

HOTP codes use a counter that advances with each code; TOTP codes rotate over time.

docs.title: Account operations
docs.text:
For each account, you can:

  • Rename
  • Delete

When you use the codes:

  • TOTP entries refresh automatically according to their period.
  • Click a TOTP or HOTP code chip to copy the current code to the clipboard.
  • For HOTP, clicking the chip also calculates the next counter-based code.

docs.title: Locked state
docs.text: When the OATH applet is protected, unlock it before viewing account data.

docs.title: Registration requirement
docs.text: The board must be registered in PicoKey App before you can manage accounts. Otherwise, account actions are restricted.

docs.title: FIDO Dashboard
docs.text: The FIDO dashboard is the starting point for FIDO features in PicoKey App.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
From here, you can open:

  • Passkeys management
  • OTP slots management
  • OATH accounts management
  • Initialization and provisioning actions

Choose the area that matches what you want to manage on the connected device.

docs.title: Device information shown
docs.text:
The dashboard also shows FIDO device details, including:

  • AAGUID
  • Maximum credBlob size
  • Number of largeBlobs entries
  • largeBlob storage usage

Use these values to check the authenticator's capabilities and storage state.

docs.title: Keyboard Interface
docs.text:
The Keyboard Interface switch controls the USB keyboard interface through the device's PHY settings.

This interface is used by the OTP slots to type configured output when the device button is pressed. When it is disabled, PicoKey App disables the keyboard-dependent actions for slots 1 to 4:

  • Static Password
  • HOTP
  • Yubico OTP

Challenge-response remains available because it does not type through the USB keyboard interface. Re-enable the switch before configuring or using the keyboard-dependent OTP actions.

docs.title: Options and extensions
docs.text:
The dashboard lists:

  • Pico FIDO options reported by the authenticator
  • Supported FIDO/WebAuthn extensions

Options shown in green are active on the connected device.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The available actions depend on the installed firmware.
  • Some actions require PIN verification before the app shows sensitive data.

docs.title: Pico FIDO Initialization
docs.text:
Use PicoKey App to set the security initialization and provisioning options for Pico FIDO.

These options are applied during initialization and shape the authenticator's security model.

docs.title: PIN
docs.text:
Set the authenticator's user verification PIN here.

  • The PIN is required for user verification when enabled
  • It protects resident credentials and sensitive operations

Warning

Losing the PIN may permanently lock access to credentials.

docs.title: Attestation
docs.text:
Enable authenticator attestation here.

When enabled:

  • The authenticator presents an attestation certificate
  • Relying parties can identify the device type

Note

Attestation may reduce user privacy depending on the relying party.

docs.title: Minimum PIN length
docs.text:
Set the minimum allowed PIN length.

  • Enforced at PIN setup time
  • Applies to all future PIN changes

Tip

Longer PINs significantly improve resistance against guessing attacks.

docs.title: PIN complexity policy
docs.text:
When supported by the firmware, PIN Complexity Policy lets you set a policy URL and choose one of these requirements. Enable the policy switch before applying the URL or selecting a requirement:

  • upper letters
  • lower letters
  • mixed letters
  • digits only
  • alphanumeric
  • alphanumeric plus symbols

The policy is enforced by the authenticator when PINs are created or changed.

docs.title: RP IDs restriction
docs.text:
Restrict which Relying Party IDs the authenticator accepts.

  • RP IDs must be explicitly listed
  • Multiple RP IDs are separated by commas

Danger

Incorrect RP ID configuration may prevent authentication on valid services.

docs.title: FIDO behavior toggles
docs.text:
The initialization panel can also expose:

  • Enable Discoverable Credentials (rk): enables or disables resident credential creation.
  • Make Cred UV Not Required: allows credential creation without user verification when the relying-party request and device policy permit it.
  • Enable Always UV: requires user verification for applicable operations.

Use Apply Changes after changing these switches. Verify the resulting options on the FIDO Dashboard before enrolling production credentials.

docs.title: Initialization process
docs.text:
After choosing the options you need:

  • Click Apply Changes
  • The device is provisioned with the selected security parameters

Warning

Initialization is irreversible without a full device reset.

docs.title: Registration requirement
docs.text: Register the board in PicoKey App before using this panel; otherwise, initialization actions are disabled.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Security initialization defines the trust model of Pico FIDO, so choose these options to set:

  • Strong authentication guarantees
  • Resistance against firmware tampering
  • Controlled use of attestation and PIN policies

docs.title: Passkeys
docs.text: Use the Passkeys panel to review and manage resident FIDO credentials stored on the device.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The panel lists resident FIDO credentials with their metadata, and provides actions for each credential.

  • Credential source and relying party information
  • Username / user handle when available
  • Per-credential management actions

docs.title: Per-credential actions
docs.text:
Each row includes these actions when they are available:

  • Copy Credential ID
  • Large Blob: manage the credential’s Large Blob when it has one
  • Credential lifecycle (gear): set or change an expiration date, or revoke the credential
  • Download Credential Metadata (JSON or CSV)
  • Export Credential: export the credential to Vault when an enrolled Vault is available
  • Delete Credential

Credential metadata downloads contain administrative fields such as the RP, user information, and credential ID. They are separate from Export Credential, which creates an opaque Vault package. Revoked credentials cannot be changed.

docs.title: Individual credential lifecycle
docs.text:
Click the gear to open the Manage Credential dialog for the selected credential.

  • Set expiration stores an optional expiration date and time. The board requires a configured RTC to set this value. When the RTC reaches the expiration time, the credential becomes EXPIRED and Pico FIDO rejects assertions for it.
  • Revoke immediately marks the credential as REVOKED and prevents it from being used for assertions.

Expired and revoked credentials remain listed so their status can be audited; they are not deleted automatically. The operation applies only to the selected credential, so other credentials on the board remain unaffected. Neither operation removes the corresponding registration at a relying party, and the current firmware does not provide a way to reactivate an expired or revoked credential.

docs.title: Credential details shown
docs.text:
The list also shows metadata that can help with administration and troubleshooting:

  • Algorithm
  • Curve
  • credProtect extension value, when present
  • Credential status (ACTIVE, EXPIRED, or REVOKED)
  • Credential source (Native or Imported)
  • Whether signCount is enabled or disabled
  • Creation date when the device RTC was available when the credential was created
  • Expiration date when one has been configured

docs.title: Selection and bulk operations
docs.text:
Filter credentials by common fields such as:

  • RP (Relying Party)
  • User
  • Credential ID
  • Other searchable credential fields shown in the table

Each row has a selection switch. To apply an action to several credentials, use Select all for the displayed results, then choose an action from the bulk menu:

  • Export selected: exports the selected credentials to Vault using the chosen export algorithm.
  • Revoke selected: revokes the selected credentials so they cannot be used for assertions again.
  • Delete selected: deletes the selected resident credentials from the board.

Each row also has its own Vault export button, so bulk selection is optional. Administrative operations also include deleting all credentials for a specific RP.

docs.title: Vault export
docs.text:
When the board is enrolled and the passkey session is unlocked, the panel can export selected resident credentials to the Pico Vault. Choose the encryption profile before exporting:

  • ChaChaPoly
  • AES-GCM
  • ChaChaPoly + AES-GCM
  • AES-GCM + ChaChaPoly

The Vault export stores an opaque package and credential display metadata in the local Vault store. It does not export the private key as plaintext. A credential already exported to the active Vault is skipped.

docs.title: Locked state
docs.text:
When credentials are protected by PIN or policy, the panel requires user verification before showing sensitive data.

Note

Exact fields and actions depend on the installed firmware.

docs.title: Slots
docs.text:
Use the slot management view in PicoKey App to configure OTP and related features.

Each slot can hold an OTP, static password, or related function supported by the device firmware.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Slots view shows all available slots supported by the device.

Each slot is either:

  • empty; or
  • configured with a specific function.

Slots are independent from each other and can be configured individually.

docs.title: Slot activation
docs.text:
To activate a slot, press the BOOTSEL button N consecutive times, where N is the slot number.

  • Slot 1: press once
  • Slot 2: press twice in a row
  • Slot 3: press three times in a row
  • And so on for higher slot numbers

Note

Presses must be consecutive so the device can map the sequence to the correct slot.

For Static Password, YubiOTP, and HOTP slots, activation types the configured output on the host through the USB keyboard interface.

Note

This keyboard-style output does not apply to Challenge-Response slots.

docs.title: Empty
docs.text: An empty slot has no configuration, so you can provision it for a new function. Triggering it has no effect.

docs.title: Configured
docs.text:
A configured slot shows its number, function, and any other available details:

  • The slot number
  • The configuration type
  • Additional information depending on the configuration

Examples of configured slots include:

  • Static password
  • YubicoOTP

Note

The exact slot capabilities depend on the firmware running on the device.

docs.title: Slot actions
docs.text:
Use the icons to configure or manage a slot:

  • Challenge-response
  • Static password
  • HOTP
  • YubiOTP
  • Delete slot configuration

docs.title: Delete slot configuration
docs.text:
Delete the slot configuration to:

  • Returns the slot to the empty state
  • Removes all associated data

Danger

Deleting a slot configuration permanently erases all data stored in the slot.

docs.title: Registration requirement
docs.text: Register the board in PicoKey App before using the slot actions; otherwise, the buttons are disabled.

docs.title: User PIN (Vendor Feature)
docs.text: The User PIN feature adds a second FIDO PIN context with its own permissions.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This feature supports multi-user FIDO passkeys by letting an Admin choose which operations the User context can perform.

Typical use case: an organization configures the key with a manager/admin account first, then hands the key to a worker account with reduced administration permissions.

docs.title: What this feature adds
docs.text:
This vendor extension is implemented by PicoKey firmware and PicoKey App; it is outside the standard FIDO behavior.

The device can operate with two PIN contexts:

  • Admin PIN: full management permissions.
  • User PIN: restricted permissions defined by the Admin.

Each context has its own PIN value.

docs.title: Permission model
docs.text:
When User PIN is enabled, Admin can set which Passkeys management actions the User context may perform.

The following permissions can be enabled or disabled for User context:

  • Create credentials
  • Credential management
  • Authentication
  • Large Blob write
  • Configure authenticator
  • Persistent credential management
  • Reset authenticator

By default:

  • All permissions are enabled by default.
  • Authentication is always enabled and cannot be effectively removed, otherwise the user would not be able to authenticate to any service.

Admin context keeps full access regardless of User restrictions.

docs.title: Default context behavior
docs.text:
• If User PIN is disabled: only Admin context is active.
  • If User PIN is enabled: device defaults to User context after each connect/reconnect.

When User PIN is enabled, PicoKey App opens in User context after each connection unless you switch to Admin.

docs.title: Context switching in PicoKey App
docs.text:
Switch contexts in FIDO > Passkeys.

The switch is available only after a PIN has been configured for the active context.

Operational sequence:

  1. Connect device (loads User context by default when enabled).
  2. Unlock first (context switch requires an unlocked state).
  3. Switch context to Admin when elevated actions are required.
  4. If needed, unlock with the PIN of the selected context to continue protected operations.

If you need to disable User PIN, switch to Admin context first, then disable User PIN.

docs.title: Practical notes
docs.text:
• Keep the Admin and User PINs as separate credentials.
  • Give the User context only the permissions it needs.
  • If management actions are unavailable, check the current context before troubleshooting.

docs.title: FIDO Vault
docs.text: The FIDO > Vault panel manages local backups of credentials exported from an enrolled Pico FIDO device. It is the desktop part of the Pico Vault workflow; it does not enroll a board.

docs.title: Before opening the panel
docs.text:
1. Register the board in PicoKey App.
  2. Install and run the standalone pico-vault-enroller.
  3. Enroll the board with an encrypted enrollment envelope.
  4. Unlock FIDO > Passkeys with the device PIN.

Select FIDO > Vault and click Refresh. The panel shows the Vault ID when the board is enrolled. If it is not enrolled, the panel points to the standalone enroller.

The local store can contain packages from several Vault IDs. The panel groups them by ID and shows the active board's Vault ID at the top.

docs.title: Export a passkey
docs.text:
From FIDO > Passkeys, choose one or more resident credentials and select an export profile:

  • ChaChaPoly
  • AES-GCM
  • ChaChaPoly + AES-GCM
  • AES-GCM + ChaChaPoly

Use the credential's Vault export action or Export selected. The app saves the opaque Vault package and display metadata in its local Vault store. A credential already stored in the active Vault is not exported again.

The local store can display the relying party, user information, algorithm, board serial, and Vault ID. It does not turn the package into a plaintext private key.

docs.title: Import a passkey
docs.text:
On the destination board:

  1. Enroll it with the same enrollment envelope.
  2. Unlock FIDO > Passkeys.
  3. Open FIDO > Vault and click Refresh.
  4. Select a credential and use its import button, or choose Import selected.

You can import only packages whose Vault ID matches the active board. Packages from other Vaults remain visible in their groups, but their import actions are disabled. Imported credentials appear in the destination's passkey list as separate resident credentials.

You can use the same encrypted enrollment envelope for multiple boards. They will report the same Vault ID and can exchange exported credentials through that Vault domain. Create another envelope only when you want a separate Vault domain.

Use Select all and Import selected for a bulk import from the active Vault group. The panel also provides an import button for each eligible row.

docs.title: Delete local Vault records
docs.text: The row delete button and Delete selected remove packages from the local Vault store. They leave any credential already imported into a board in place, so deleting a package affects the backup store rather than the device.

docs.title: Security and recovery
docs.text: Protect the enrollment JSON, its passphrase, device PIN, and exported packages separately. PicoKey App cannot reset a lost enrollment passphrase. If a package or enrollment secret is exposed, treat it as a recovery incident and rotate the Vault domain according to the Vault operations guide.

docs.title: Slot: Challenge-Response
docs.text: A Challenge-Response slot uses a host-driven mechanism: the host creates a challenge, the device processes it, and the host verifies the response.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The host application drives authentication using a secret stored on the device. It verifies the response itself, so it does not need to keep a reusable secret.

docs.title: Authentication model
docs.text:
The host first generates a random challenge and sends it to the device. The device uses the slot secret to process the challenge, then returns a response for the host to verify. Authentication succeeds only when that response matches the expected value.

Note

The device does not decide whether authentication succeeds. Validation is entirely performed by the host.

docs.title: Key
docs.text:
Enter the secret key used to process challenges. The device stores it securely, limits its length according to the slot implementation, and does not return it in plaintext after configuration.

Warning

Losing the key means the challenge-response authentication cannot be validated anymore.

docs.title: Require touch
docs.text:
When enabled, the device waits for a physical touch or confirmation before it generates a response.

Note

Requiring touch prevents unattended or automated authentication attempts.

docs.title: Save and cancel
docs.text:
• Save stores the slot configuration permanently.
  • Cancel discards the changes.

Danger

Saving overwrites any existing slot configuration.

docs.title: Security properties
docs.text:
Random challenges help prevent replay attacks. The slot does not send a static secret over the interface, and you can require user presence before it responds.

Warning

Security depends entirely on correct challenge generation and verification on the host side.

docs.title: Typical use cases
docs.text:
Challenge-Response slots are commonly used for:

  • Device-bound authentication for custom applications
  • Licensing or entitlement checks
  • Secure device identification
  • Anti-cloning mechanisms

Tip

Always use cryptographically strong random challenges.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
The device does not verify the response, the protocol is application-specific, and the host must implement verification.

Note

This slot is intended for advanced users and custom integrations.

docs.title: Slot: HOTP
docs.text: An HOTP (HMAC-Based One-Time Password) slot generates a numeric code from a shared secret and types it as keyboard input when triggered.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The device stores a shared secret and uses it to generate HOTP codes when the slot is activated. It types each code through its USB keyboard interface, and a remote system verifies the code using the same secret.

docs.title: Activation mechanism
docs.text:
The HOTP slot is activated through the OTP / button interface.

Press the BOOTSEL button N times, where N is the slot number. The device then generates the next HOTP value and types it into the host as keyboard input.

Note

No dedicated software is required on the host beyond USB HID keyboard support.

docs.title: Key
docs.text:
Enter the shared secret used to generate HOTP values. The device stores it securely and does not return it after setup; the slot implementation also limits its maximum length.

Warning

If the secret is lost, the HOTP sequence cannot be regenerated or validated.

docs.title: Number of digits
docs.text:
Choose how many digits the generated code contains:

Supported values:

  • 6 digits
  • 8 digits

Note

The verifier must be configured to expect the same number of digits.

docs.title: Append Enter
docs.text:
When enabled, the device sends Enter after the code, which can submit a form automatically.

Tip

Enable this option when authenticating into login forms or terminals.

docs.title: Save and cancel
docs.text:
• Save stores the HOTP configuration permanently.
  • Cancel discards the changes.

Danger

Saving overwrites any existing slot configuration.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
Each activation generates a new code. The device keeps the shared secret private and emits the code only as keyboard input.

Warning

HOTP counters must remain synchronized with the verification system.

docs.title: Typical use cases
docs.text:
Use HOTP slots for:

  • Two-factor authentication systems
  • Legacy systems without TOTP support
  • Offline authentication scenarios
  • Environments requiring keyboard-based OTP input

Tip

Ensure proper counter resynchronization policies on the server side.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
HOTP uses a counter rather than time, so the device and verifier can become desynchronized. The verifier must check each code, and the device emits codes only through the keyboard interface.

Note

For time-based OTP, consider using TOTP-capable solutions if available.

docs.title: Slot: Static Password
docs.text: A Static Password slot stores a fixed password and types it as keyboard input when triggered.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The device stores a fixed password and types it through its USB keyboard interface when the slot is activated. This works with systems that accept keyboard input.

docs.title: Activation mechanism
docs.text:
The Static Password slot is activated through the OTP / button interface.

Press the BOOTSEL button N times, where N is the slot number. The device then types the stored password into the host as keyboard input.

Note

No software on the host is required beyond standard USB HID keyboard support.

docs.title: Password
docs.text:
Enter the fixed password for this slot. The device stores it securely and does not return it after setup; the slot implementation also limits its maximum length.

Warning

Losing the password means it cannot be recovered from the device.

docs.title: Append Enter
docs.text:
When enabled, the device sends Enter after the password, which can submit a form automatically.

Tip

Enable this option when logging into terminals or login forms.

docs.title: Keyboard layout
docs.text:
The selected layout controls how characters map to keyboard scancodes. Match it to the host's keyboard layout to avoid incorrect characters.

Warning

A mismatched keyboard layout may produce incorrect characters.

docs.title: Save and cancel
docs.text:
• Save stores the password permanently in the slot.
  • Cancel discards the changes.

Danger

Saving overwrites any existing slot configuration.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
The device does not expose the password through software interfaces; it types it through the keyboard interface and does not require host authentication to trigger the slot.

Warning

Anyone with physical access to the device may trigger the slot.

docs.title: Typical use cases
docs.text:
Static Password slots can help with:

  • Login to systems without password managers
  • Unlocking encrypted volumes
  • Entering recovery passwords
  • Automating repetitive authentication steps

Tip

Use Static Password slots only on trusted systems.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
This slot does not use challenge-response or host-side verification. Because the password is fixed and typed visibly, it can be exposed through shoulder surfing or screen recording.

Note

This slot prioritizes convenience over cryptographic authentication.

docs.title: Slot: Yubico OTP
docs.text: A Yubico OTP slot generates one-time passwords according to the Yubico OTP specification and types them as keyboard input when triggered.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The device stores Yubico-compatible identifiers and secret keys, then uses them to generate OTP values when the slot is activated. It types each code through its USB keyboard interface for services that support Yubico OTP.

docs.title: Activation mechanism
docs.text:
The Yubico OTP slot is activated through the OTP / button interface.

Press the BOOTSEL button N times, where N is the slot number. The device then generates a Yubico OTP and types it into the host as keyboard input.

Note

No additional software is required on the host beyond USB HID keyboard support.

docs.title: Public ID
docs.text: Enter the public identifier that the verification service uses to identify the device. It is sent in clear as part of the OTP and is limited in length by the Yubico specification.

docs.title: Private ID (hex)
docs.text:
Enter the private identifier in hexadecimal format. The device stores it securely and uses it internally when generating OTP values.

Warning

The private ID cannot be retrieved once stored.

docs.title: Key (hex)
docs.text:
Enter the secret key in hexadecimal format. The device stores it securely and does not expose it outside the device.

Danger

Losing the secret key prevents OTP verification and cannot be recovered.

docs.title: Append Enter
docs.text:
When enabled, the device sends Enter after the OTP, which can submit a form automatically.

Tip

Enable this option when authenticating on web login forms.

docs.title: Save and cancel
docs.text:
• Save stores the Yubico OTP configuration permanently.
  • Cancel discards the changes.

Danger

Saving overwrites any existing slot configuration.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
The slot follows the Yubico OTP specification and keeps its secrets out of software interfaces. It emits OTPs only as keyboard input.

Warning

Anyone with physical access to the device may trigger OTP generation.

docs.title: Typical use cases
docs.text:
Use Yubico OTP slots for:

  • Authentication against Yubico-compatible servers
  • Legacy systems using Yubico OTP
  • Environments requiring keyboard-based OTP input

Tip

Ensure the verification backend is correctly configured with matching identifiers and keys.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
The service must support Yubico OTP, and the device emits the code through its keyboard interface without host-side confirmation.

Note

This slot is intended for compatibility with existing Yubico OTP infrastructures.

docs.title: Pico HSM Cipher
docs.text:
Use HSM > Management > Cipher in PicoKey App to run operations with an existing key.

The Cipher tab runs cryptographic operations using the selected Key ID.

docs.title: Prerequisite
docs.text:
Before you run an operation:

  1. Go to HSM > Management.
  2. Enter PIN.
  3. Click Unlock.
  4. Wait until keys are loaded.
  5. If needed, expand Session and use Reload / Change PIN.
  6. Use a valid Key ID.

docs.title: Main controls
docs.text:
• Operation: Sign, Decrypt, Encrypt, MAC, KDF
  • Algorithm: available values depend on key type and selected operation
  • Key ID: key handle used by the operation
  • I/O flow: File flow or Text box flow
  • Run Cipher: executes the selected operation

docs.title: I/O flow
docs.text: Choose between two input and output modes.

docs.title: File flow
docs.text:
Use files as input and output.

The file flow reads from Input file or the drop zone, then writes the result to Output file. Use the Browse buttons to choose the paths.

docs.title: Text box flow
docs.text:
Use a single text area for both input and output.

Enter plaintext, data, or signing input in the text box. After the operation, the app replaces the input with the result. Use Text input/output is hex to switch between plain text and hexadecimal input/output.

docs.title: Operation-specific fields
docs.text:
• Encrypt/Decrypt with AEAD/stream-like modes can require IV / Nonce (hex) and optional AAD (text or hex).
  • MAC uses file/text input and writes tag output.
  • KDF can include Output length (bytes) and, for PBKDF2, PBKDF2 iterations.

docs.title: EdDSA keys (ed25519, ed448)
docs.text:
• Only Sign is available.
  • The only signature algorithm is EDDSA.

docs.title: Other ECC keys
docs.text:
• Sign supports:
  • EC-RAW
  • EC-SHA1
  • EC-SHA224
  • EC-SHA256
  • EC-SHA384
  • EC-SHA512

docs.title: RSA keys
docs.text:
• Sign supports:
  • RSA-RAW
  • RSA-PKCS1
  • RSA-PKCS1-SHA1
  • RSA-PKCS1-SHA224
  • RSA-PKCS1-SHA256
  • RSA-PKCS1-SHA384
  • RSA-PKCS1-SHA512
  • RSA-PSS
  • RSA-PSS-SHA1
  • RSA-PSS-SHA224
  • RSA-PSS-SHA256
  • RSA-PSS-SHA384

  • RSA-PSS-SHA512

  • Decrypt supports:

  • RSA-RAW
  • RSA-PKCS1
  • RSA-OAEP

docs.title: AES keys (symmetric keys)
docs.text:
• Encrypt / Decrypt support:
  • CHACHAPOLY
  • AES-ECB
  • AES-CBC (input length must be a multiple of 16 bytes)
  • AES-OFB
  • AES-CFB
  • AES-GCM
  • AES-CCM
  • AES-CTR

  • AES-XTS

  • MAC supports:

  • CMAC
  • HMAC-SHA1
  • HMAC-SHA224
  • HMAC-SHA256
  • HMAC-SHA384

  • HMAC-SHA512

  • KDF supports:

  • HKDF-SHA256
  • HKDF-SHA384
  • HKDF-SHA512
  • PBKDF2-SHA1
  • PBKDF2-SHA224
  • PBKDF2-SHA256
  • PBKDF2-SHA384
  • PBKDF2-SHA512
  • X963-SHA1
  • X963-SHA224
  • X963-SHA256
  • X963-SHA384
  • X963-SHA512

Note

The selector omits algorithms for operations that the selected key type does not support.

docs.title: Pico HSM Hierarchical Deterministic (HD / BIP32)
docs.text:
Use HSM > Management > BIP32 in PicoKey App to manage hierarchical deterministic keys.

The BIP32 tab lets you:

  • Initialize master material
  • Derive child keys / XPUB data by derivation path
  • Decode XPUB
  • Sign using a derivation path

docs.title: Prerequisite
docs.text:
Before running a BIP32 operation:

  1. Go to HSM > Management.
  2. Enter PIN.
  3. Click Unlock.
  4. Wait until keys are loaded.
  5. Use the BIP32 tab.

docs.title: Main controls
docs.text:
The main controls are:

  • Operation: Initialize, Derive, Decode XPUB, Sign
  • Master ID: identifier that binds a master node to its curve type (0-255)
  • Derivation path: path format such as m/44h/0h/0h/0/0
  • Run BIP32: executes the selected operation

Supported master curve types:

  • secp256k1
  • secp256r1
  • Symmetric key (SLIP)

docs.title: Initialize
docs.text:
Initialize HD material for the selected master ID.

Visible fields:

  • Curve (example shown: secp256k1)
  • Seed file (optional): optional seed input from file
  • Derivation path

If you leave Seed file (optional) empty, the device generates the seed according to its firmware behavior.

docs.title: Derive
docs.text:
Derives BIP32 child output from a derivation path and selected master.

Visible fields:

  • Derivation path
  • Input/Output (text): output is written in the same box
  • Text input/output is hex toggle

After execution, the bottom message area shows status information, including the depth, child, and fingerprint.

docs.title: Decode XPUB
docs.text:
Decode an XPUB value to view its metadata as JSON.

Visible output:

  • depth
  • fingerprint
  • child
  • chain
  • public

The decoded payload is shown in Decoded XPUB (JSON).

docs.title: Sign with derivation path
docs.text:
BIP32 signing uses the selected master plus derivation path.

As in the Cipher tab, signing supports both text-box and file flows.

docs.title: Sign with text box flow
docs.text: Enter data in Input/Output (text). After signing, the app replaces it with the output. Use Text input/output is hex to switch between plain text and hexadecimal input/output.

docs.title: Sign with file flow
docs.text: Choose the file to sign with Data file (required for Sign), then select a destination with Output file. The Browse buttons open the file picker.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Use Master ID to keep multiple independent HD roots, each associated with its selected curve type.
  • A valid derivation path is required for derive/sign operations.
  • BIP32 operations are available only after a successful unlock.

docs.title: Pico HSM Initialization
docs.text:
Use PicoKey App to set the security initialization options for Pico HSM.

These settings define PIN policies, key protection, and recovery options.

docs.title: User PIN
docs.text:
Set the primary user PIN here.

  • Required for cryptographic operations
  • Protects private keys and stored objects

Tip

The default PIN is 648219.

docs.title: SO PIN
docs.text:
Set the Security Officer PIN here.

  • Used for administrative operations
  • Required for certain reset and recovery commands

Note

The SO PIN should be stored separately from the user PIN.

docs.title: PIN retries
docs.text:
Choose how many incorrect PIN attempts are allowed.

  • Applies to both user PIN and SO PIN
  • Exceeding the limit blocks access

Danger

Exceeding retry limits may permanently lock the device.

docs.title: DKEK shares
docs.text:
Enables Distributed Key Encryption Key (DKEK) shares.

  • Splits the encryption key into multiple shares
  • Requires a threshold number of shares for recovery

Note

This option is only useful when no key domains are configured. Otherwise, each key domain can be configured independently with different DKEK shares.

docs.title: PUK authentications
docs.text:
Set how many public keys can be used for authentication.

  • Used when PKA is enabled
  • Adds an additional authentication mechanism without PIN

docs.title: PUK minimum authentications
docs.text:
Set the minimum number of public keys required for authentication.

  • Used when PKA is enabled

docs.title: Key domains
docs.text:
Enables key domain separation.

  • Keys are grouped into isolated domains
  • Access policies can differ per domain

docs.title: Reset retry counter command
docs.text:
Allows a command to reset the retry counter when the PIN is blocked, and can also allow a PIN reset.

  • Useful for controlled recovery scenarios

Danger

If this option is disabled, Pico HSM will not be recoverable if PIN locked. In this case, a Factory Reset will be necessary and all keys and data will be lost permanently.

docs.title: Transport PIN
docs.text:
Allows you to set a temporary PIN for transport or provisioning.

Warning

Transport PINs should be changed immediately after deployment.

docs.title: PKA replaceable
docs.text: Allows public-key authentication data to be replaced.

docs.title: Combined PIN & PKA authentication
docs.text:
Require both the PIN and public-key authentication.

  • Provides multi-factor protection

docs.title: Reset Retry Counter only resets error counter
docs.text:
The Reset Retry command clears the retry counter without changing the PIN.

Note

This option is usable only when Reset Retry Counter command is enabled.

docs.title: Force Device Certificate
docs.text: Downloads and re-signs the attestation certificate. Use this only if you encounter issues with third-party applications.

docs.title: Initialization process
docs.text:
After setting the parameters:

  • Click Initialize
  • The device is provisioned with the selected security configuration

Danger

Some options cannot be changed without reinitializing the device.

docs.title: Pico HSM Key Management
docs.text:
Use HSM > Management > Keys in PicoKey App to manage keys, domains, certificates, and data objects.

From this view, you can:

  • Unlocking the HSM session and using the collapsed session panel
  • Key domain setup and DKEK workflows
  • Key generation/import
  • Key, certificate, and data object management

docs.title: Load management session
docs.text:
When you open HSM > Management, PicoKey App first shows the unlock view.

  1. Enter the user PIN.
  2. Click Unlock.
  3. Wait until key loading finishes.

After unlocking, the Session section collapses to save space.

Expand Session again to access maintenance actions:

docs.title: Session buttons
docs.text:
• Reload: reloads keys/domains/certificates for the current authenticated session.
  • Change PIN: opens the PIN change flow.

If the PIN is blocked, the panel also shows these recovery actions:

  • Unblock PIN
  • Reset Retries

Note

If unlock fails, management data is not loaded.

docs.title: Keys view layout
docs.text:
The Keys tab is divided into two areas:

  • Left panel: hierarchical tree (No domain, Domain N, keys, certificates, data objects)
  • Right panel: context actions and details for the selected item

Use the tabs at the top to switch between:

  • Keys: key tree and key/domain actions
  • Cipher: cryptographic operations view
  • BIP32: hierarchical deterministic key view

For cipher operations, see Cipher.

docs.title: 1) Setup a new key domain
docs.text:
Select a domain marked as (not created).

When a domain is marked (not created), you can:

  • Set up: creates the key domain.
  • Create DKEK Share: creates a DKEK share file in .pbe format so it can be imported later.

docs.title: 2) Create DKEK share (.pbe)
docs.text:
Click Create DKEK Share to open the dialog and create a DKEK share.

Dialog fields:

  • Output file: destination path for the generated .pbe file.
  • Browse: opens file picker for output location.
  • Password: password used to protect the DKEK share.
  • Confirm password: must match the password.

docs.title: 3) Import missing DKEK share(s)
docs.text:
If a domain shows Missing 1 DKEK, click Import DKEK.

A password dialog is shown:

The app uses the share password to load the DKEK share into the domain.

docs.title: 4) Domain ready state
docs.text:
Once the domain has the required DKEK material, it shows a KCV and these actions:

Domain buttons:

  • Generate: create a new key directly in that domain
  • Import Key: import an existing key into the selected domain
  • Clear: remove DKEK material for that domain session/state
  • Import P12: import key/certificate material from PKCS#12
  • Delete: remove the domain configuration

Danger

Deleting a domain or clearing critical domain material can make keys unavailable.

docs.title: Generate key
docs.text:
From a ready domain, click Generate.

Visible parameters in the dialog:

  • Key type/family/curve selectors (example shown: ECC + Edwards + ed25519)
  • Label: local alias for easier identification
  • Use Counter: usage limit slider (Unlimited when not limited). This is a decrementing counter: each key use decreases it by 1, and when it reaches 0 the key can no longer be used.
  • Purpose flags: Default, Derive, Wrap, Sign, Encrypt/Decrypt, Custom
  • Algorithms: algorithm set bound to key usage policy

docs.title: Import PKCS#12 (P12)
docs.text:
From domain actions, click Import P12.

Dialog fields:

  • P12 Password: optional password for the PKCS#12 container
  • DKEK file + Browse: select DKEK file used during import
  • DKEK Password: password used for PBE when required

docs.title: Key details actions
docs.text:
Select a key in the tree to view its metadata and actions in the right panel.

Common key actions:

  • Export Public: exports the public part of the selected key
  • Export Certificate: exports associated certificate when available
  • Change Label: updates key label
  • Delete: deletes the selected key

Conditional action:

  • Wrap: wraps (exports in protected form) keys marked as exportable/wrappable

Displayed metadata includes:

  • Key ID, Type, Curve, Size
  • Label, Use Counter, Purposes
  • Certificate references (Cert CHR, Cert CAR) when present

Warning

Delete is irreversible. Ensure backups or wrapped exports exist before removal.

docs.title: Certificate details
docs.text:
Select a certificate under Certificates (such as Device, CVCA, or DVCA) to view its metadata in the right panel.

Visible fields:

  • Label: certificate alias shown in the UI
  • Cert CHR: certificate holder reference
  • Cert CAR: certificate authority reference

Action:

  • Export Certificate: exports the selected certificate file.

Note

This action exports certificate data only, not the private key.

docs.title: Certificate import
docs.text:
Select the root Certificates node to open certificate import actions.

Action:

  • Import Certificate: imports a certificate into the certificates store shown in the tree.
  • Delete Certificate: removes the selected certificate entry.

docs.title: Data objects (Import Object)
docs.text:
Select Data Objects > Public to import public data objects.

Available actions:

  • Import Public Object: imports a public data object from a file.
  • Import Public Hex: imports a public data object from hexadecimal input.
  • Import Private Object: imports a private data object from a file.
  • Import Private Hex: imports a private data object from hexadecimal input.

Data Objects > Private is reserved for private objects and follows the same tree navigation pattern.

docs.title: Registration requirement
docs.text: Register the board in PicoKey App before using this panel; otherwise, management actions are restricted.

docs.title: OpenPGP Management
docs.text: Use OpenPGP > Management in PicoKey App to check card status and manage OpenPGP keys.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The view groups its controls into:

  • OpenPGP Card Status (card metadata and PIN/session state)
  • Operation modes:
  • Basic (global key operations)
  • Advanced (slot-level key operations)
  • Key slots:
  • Signature (SIG)
  • Decryption (DEC)
  • Authentication (AUT)
  • Maintenance actions:
  • Lock
  • Change PIN
  • Factory Reset

docs.title: Access model (PW1 / PW3)
docs.text:
OpenPGP management can be unlocked with:

  • PW1 (user context)
  • PW3 (admin context)

Unlock with PW3 to generate or export keys and edit protected card settings.

With only PW1 unlocked, you can still read the panel, while admin-level changes remain restricted.

docs.title: Card status
docs.text:
The OpenPGP Card Status section shows:

  • Application ID
  • Version
  • Signature counter
  • Signature PIN mode (toggle)
  • KDF state
  • Session state (for example Unlocked (PW3))
  • Cardholder name
  • Language prefs
  • URL of public key
  • Login data
  • PIN retries for PW1, RC, and PW3

The panel also reminds you that:

  • Tip: Click editable values to edit

Note

Fields and editability depend on firmware capabilities and the current authentication state.

docs.title: Operation modes
docs.text: OpenPGP management provides two operation modes:

docs.title: Basic mode
docs.text:
In Basic mode, each key operation applies to the entire OpenPGP keyset:

  • Generate creates/regenerates key material for all three slots (SIG, DEC, AUT).
  • Export exports public keys for all three slots in one global operation.

docs.title: Advanced mode
docs.text:
In Advanced mode, you can work with each slot separately:

  • Generate is available independently for each slot (SIG, DEC, AUT).
  • Export can be executed for a single slot, exporting only that slot's public key.

Warning

Generating a key always replaces existing key material in the target scope (all slots in Basic, one slot in Advanced).

docs.title: Key slots (SIG / DEC / AUT)
docs.text:
For each slot, the panel shows:

  • Fingerprint (or [none] when empty)
  • Key attributes selector (algorithm/key type)
  • Key present state/date (or Empty)
  • Generate button (in Advanced mode)
  • Export action (in Advanced mode)
  • UIF toggle (user interaction control)

Typical state examples:

  • SIG is populated (ed25519)
  • DEC is populated (x25519)
  • AUT is empty and set to RSA 2048

docs.title: Public key export format
docs.text:
When exporting OpenPGP public keys, PicoKey App saves them in:

  • .asc format
  • ASCII armored representation

Note

This is the standard armored OpenPGP public key format used by most OpenPGP tools, both for global export (Basic) and per-slot export (Advanced).

docs.title: Lock
docs.text:
• Lock closes the current OpenPGP management session.
  • Sensitive actions may require re-authentication afterwards.

docs.title: Change PIN
docs.text:
• Change PIN opens the PIN update workflow.
  • Use it to rotate user/admin credentials according to your policy.

docs.title: Factory reset
docs.text:
• Factory Reset wipes OpenPGP card data and keys (admin/destructive operation).

Danger

Factory reset is destructive and cannot be undone.

docs.title: Registration requirement
docs.text: Register the board in PicoKey App before using this panel; otherwise, controls are restricted.

docs.title: PIV
docs.text: Use OpenPGP > PIV in PicoKey App to view PIV status and manage PIV slots.

docs.title: PIV status
docs.text:
The PIV Status panel shows:

  • Version
  • Serial
  • Retry counters for:
  • PIN
  • PUK
  • MGM
  • Default credential indicators (PIN Default, PUK Default, MGM Default)
  • Session action: Unlock / Lock (toggle)
  • Credential actions:
  • Change PIN
  • Unblock PIN
  • Set MGM Key

Unlock the PIV session with the MGM key (management key); the user PIN does not unlock it.

Warning

Default PIN/PUK/MGM values should be changed before production use.

docs.title: Slot model
docs.text:
The view groups the standard PIV slots into:

  • Authentication Slot (9A)
  • Signature Slot (9C)
  • Key Management Slot (9D)
  • Card Authentication Slot (9E)
  • Retired Slots

For each slot, the UI shows:

  • Current algorithm
  • PIN policy
  • Touch policy
  • Origin (for example Generated or Imported)
  • Certificate state (Present or Missing)

Depending on the slot state, you may also see:

  • Generate
  • Import
  • Rotate (enabled only when applicable)
  • Attest (enabled only when applicable)
  • Export Certificate (enabled when a certificate is present)

Note

Disabled buttons indicate operations not available for the current slot state.

docs.title: Import key workflow
docs.text: Use the Import Key - Authentication (9A) dialog to load an existing private key into a PIV slot.

docs.title: Fields and controls
docs.text:
• PIN policy: defines when PIN verification is required for key usage.
  • Touch policy: defines whether user presence/touch is required.
  • Load PKCS#8: opens the file picker to load a PKCS#8 private key.
  • Loaded key: read-only indicator with the parsed key type (example shown: ECC P-256).
  • Passphrase input: unlocks the key when the PKCS#8 file is encrypted.
  • Import: confirms and writes the key to the selected slot.
  • Cancel: closes the modal without changes.

docs.title: Recommended flow
docs.text:
1. Open the target slot and click Import.
  2. Set PIN policy and Touch policy according to your security requirements.
  3. Click Load PKCS#8 and select the key file.
  4. Verify the Loaded key type is the expected one for that slot.
  5. If needed, enter the key passphrase.
  6. Click Import to apply the operation.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
• On success, the slot origin becomes Imported.
  • Slot metadata and certificate actions are refreshed based on the new key state.

Tip

Ensure the imported key matches the selected slot algorithm and certificate policy.

docs.title: Rotate key workflow
docs.text: Use the Rotate Key - Signature (9C) dialog to move an active key to another slot.

docs.title: Fields and controls
docs.text:
• To slot: destination selector (active slot, retired slot, or Delete permanently).
  • Rotate: executes the move.
  • Cancel: closes the modal without changes.

You can move an active key to another active slot or to a retired slot.

docs.title: Recommended flow
docs.text:
1. In the source slot, click Rotate.
  2. Select the destination in To slot.
  3. Confirm with Rotate.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
• The key moves to the selected destination slot.
  • Occupancy indicators in Retired Slots are updated when rotating keys into retired positions.
  • Disabled rotate actions in some slots indicate there is no key material available to move.
  • Current firmware can also move a retired key back to an active slot. Check the destination and certificate association before committing the move.
  • Choosing Delete permanently removes key material irreversibly.

docs.title: Retired slots
docs.text:
The Retired Slots panel shows:

  • Slot selector (example: Retired 4 (0x85))
  • Occupancy indicator for retired slots (R1 to R20)
  • Actions:
  • Delete
  • Rotate

Retired slots are archival positions used to store keys and certificates that are no longer active (for example, expired material kept for traceability).

Occupied retired slots are shown in green and empty ones in red.

Danger

Moving, deleting, or rotating retired slot material can permanently impact certificate history and recovery workflows.

docs.title: Registration requirement
docs.text: Register the board in PicoKey App before using this panel; otherwise, controls are restricted.

docs.title: Anti-rollback
docs.text:
Secure boot blocks unsigned firmware. Anti-rollback covers a separate case: an old image that is still correctly signed.

If an older signed image contains a serious vulnerability, secure boot alone may still allow it to run. Anti-rollback rejects firmware below a configured version floor.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
The downgrade can happen in a few steps:

  1. a device owner signs firmware version A
  2. version A later turns out to have a security bug
  3. version B fixes it
  4. an attacker with physical access flashes old signed version A

Anti-rollback closes that path when implemented and enabled correctly.

docs.title: Irreversibility
docs.text:
On RP2350-class hardware, rollback state is normally stored in one-time-programmable memory. As a result:

  • floors go up, not down
  • rollback budget is finite
  • mistakes can orphan older images permanently

Use this production feature only after you have planned for those permanent limits.

docs.title: Applicability
docs.text:
Use these questions to guide verification; commands from another project may not apply to Pico FIDO or Pico OpenPGP.

For PicoKeys firmware, verify:

  • board family
  • secure boot status
  • available provisioning tool
  • image signing flow
  • documented rollback behavior

docs.title: Operational rule
docs.text:
Raise the rollback floor only when you have a clear reason, such as:

  • a security fix blocks downgrade exploitation
  • old signed images should no longer be accepted
  • the team accepts the irreversible state change

Do not spend rollback budget on routine releases unless your process explicitly requires it.

docs.title: OTP fuses
docs.text:
Here, OTP refers to one-time-programmable chip fuses, not Yubico one-time passwords.

PicoKeys uses one-time-programmable storage on both RP2350/RP2354 and ESP32-S3 devices, although each platform names its hardware differently:

  • RP2350/RP2354: OTP rows and page locks.
  • ESP32-S3: eFuse key blocks, purpose fields, secure-boot enable bits, revoke bits, and debug-disable bits.

The source of truth for the current implementation is pico-keys-sdk/src/fs/otp.c and pico-keys-sdk/src/fs/otp.h.

Danger

These writes are permanent. A wrong OTP/eFuse write can make a board unrecoverable or unable to boot unsigned/development firmware.

docs.title: Two different OTP meanings
docs.text:
Do not confuse these:

  • Chip OTP/eFuse: irreversible hardware state used for root keys, secure boot, lockout, and sealing.
  • Pico FIDO OTP slots: Yubico OTP, HOTP, static password, and challenge-response credentials.

docs.title: Logical keys
docs.text:
PicoKeys initializes two 32-byte hardware-backed values when the relevant OTP/eFuse storage is empty:

Logical name Code name Purpose Key 1 otp_key_1 Random 32-byte key used as the device root / MKEK masking material. Key 2 otp_key_2 Generated secp256k1 private key used by rescue / secure operations that need a device private key.

The tables below show how that storage maps to each platform.

docs.title: RP2350 / RP2354
docs.text:
For RP2350-class builds, the SDK defines these rows:

Logical value OTP row Notes otp_key_1 / MKEK 0xE90 New MKEK row, 32 bytes. otp_key_2 / DEVK 0xE80 New device-key row, 32 bytes. old MKEK migration source 0xEF0 Read if present, migrated to 0xE90, then invalidated. old DEVK migration source 0xED0 Read if present, migrated to 0xE80, then invalidated.

After writing each key, the firmware also writes anti-imaging chaff:

Key row Chaff row 0xE90 0xEB0 0xE80 0xEA0

The chaff is the bitwise complement of the raw key data, written at row + 32.

docs.title: RP2350 page lock
docs.text:
After writing or migrating MKEK/DEVK material, the firmware locks the OTP page containing those rows:

Page Rows covered Why page 58 0xE80 to 0xEBF Protects MKEK/DEVK and chaff rows from later direct access according to the page lock policy.

The code calls otp_lock_page(OTP_MKEK_ROW >> 6), and 0xE90 >> 6 is page 58.

docs.title: RP2350 secure boot
docs.text:
When you enable secure boot through otp_enable_secure_boot(), the firmware modifies these RP2350 OTP areas:

Region / constant What is burned OTP_DATA_BOOTKEY0_0_ROW + 0x10 * bootkey The 32-byte secure-boot public-key hash used by the boot ROM. OTP_DATA_BOOT_FLAGS1_ROW plus redundancy rows R1 and R2 Marks the selected boot key as valid. If secure lock is requested, marks every other key invalid. OTP_DATA_CRIT1_ROW plus redundancy rows R1 through R7 Sets SECURE_BOOT_ENABLE. If secure lock is requested, also sets DEBUG_DISABLE, GLITCH_DETECTOR_ENABLE, and maximum glitch-detector sensitivity bits. OTP_DATA_PAGE1_LOCK1_ROW If secure lock is requested, makes page 1 bootloader-read-only. OTP_DATA_PAGE2_LOCK1_ROW If secure lock is requested, makes page 2 bootloader-read-only.

The secure-boot key hash currently used by the SDK is the fixed 32-byte value also present in config/rp2350/secure_boot.json.

docs.title: RP2350 anti-rollback
docs.text:
The inspected PicoKeys SDK code enables secure boot and secure lock, but it does not establish a PicoKeys-specific rollback fuse map. Rely on such a map only when the target firmware's provisioning tool exposes and documents it.

The RP2350 boot ROM has rollback support, but burning rollback state is a separate production decision from burning MKEK/DEVK and secure-boot state.

docs.title: ESP32-S3
docs.text:
ESP32-S3 does not use RP2350-style OTP rows. It uses eFuse key blocks and named eFuse fields.

For ESP builds, the SDK defines:

Logical value eFuse storage Key purpose otp_key_1 EFUSE_BLK_KEY3 Written with ESP_EFUSE_KEY_PURPOSE_USER. otp_key_2 EFUSE_BLK_KEY4 Written with ESP_EFUSE_KEY_PURPOSE_USER.

After writing either key block, the firmware write-protects:

  • the key block itself with esp_efuse_set_key_dis_write()
  • the key-purpose field with esp_efuse_set_keypurpose_dis_write()

docs.title: ESP32-S3 secure boot
docs.text:
When the firmware calls otp_enable_secure_boot() on ESP32-S3, it burns:

eFuse state What is burned unused key block selected by esp_efuse_find_unused_key_block() Stores the fixed 32-byte secure-boot digest used by PicoKeys. selected key block purpose Set to SECURE_BOOT_DIGEST0, SECURE_BOOT_DIGEST1, or SECURE_BOOT_DIGEST2 depending on bootkey index. ESP_EFUSE_SECURE_BOOT_EN Enables secure boot if not already enabled.

If a digest for the requested index already exists, the code verifies that it matches the expected PicoKeys digest before continuing.

docs.title: ESP32-S3 secure lock
docs.text:
If you request secure lock, the SDK also burns:

eFuse state Effect digest revoke bits for every non-selected digest index Revokes all secure-boot digest slots except the selected one. selected secure-boot key block write-disable Prevents rewriting the secure-boot digest block. selected secure-boot key-purpose write-disable Prevents changing the digest block purpose. ESP_EFUSE_SOFT_DIS_JTAG, when available Disables software JTAG. ESP_EFUSE_HARD_DIS_JTAG, when available Disables hardware JTAG. ESP_EFUSE_DIS_USB_JTAG, when available Disables USB JTAG. ESP_EFUSE_DIS_USB_SERIAL_JTAG, when available Disables USB serial/JTAG. ESP_EFUSE_DIS_PAD_JTAG, when available Disables pad JTAG.

The code intentionally leaves ROM download mode enabled: the call to esp_efuse_disable_rom_download_mode() is present but commented out.

docs.title: RP2350 / RP2354 burns
docs.text:
• 0xE90: MKEK / otp_key_1
  • 0xE80: DEVK / otp_key_2
  • 0xEB0: complement chaff for 0xE90
  • 0xEA0: complement chaff for 0xE80
  • page 58 lock for the MKEK/DEVK page
  • secure-boot bootkey row for the selected boot key
  • BOOT_FLAGS1 valid bit for selected boot key
  • optional BOOT_FLAGS1 invalid bits for other boot keys when secure lock is requested
  • CRIT1.SECURE_BOOT_ENABLE
  • optional CRIT1.DEBUG_DISABLE, CRIT1.GLITCH_DETECTOR_ENABLE, and glitch sensitivity when secure lock is requested
  • optional page 1 and page 2 bootloader-read-only locks when secure lock is requested

docs.title: ESP32-S3 burns
docs.text:
• EFUSE_BLK_KEY3: otp_key_1, purpose USER
  • EFUSE_BLK_KEY4: otp_key_2, purpose USER
  • write-disable for KEY3/KEY4 and their key-purpose fields
  • one secure-boot digest key block, purpose SECURE_BOOT_DIGEST0/1/2
  • ESP_EFUSE_SECURE_BOOT_EN
  • optional revoke bits for the non-selected secure-boot digests when secure lock is requested
  • optional write-disable for the selected secure-boot digest block and purpose
  • optional JTAG / USB-JTAG / USB-serial-JTAG disable bits when secure lock is requested

docs.title: Conservative operating rule
docs.text:
Before burning any fuses:

  1. confirm the exact chip family
  2. confirm the exact firmware build and provisioning command
  3. test on non-critical hardware
  4. record the before and after state

If you cannot satisfy those four conditions, do not burn fuses.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text: PicoKeys firmware provides different protections depending on the product and hardware. This model also identifies the threats that remain outside their scope, using conservative assumptions about those protections.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text:
Depending on the firmware, protected assets may include:

  • FIDO master seed
  • resident passkeys
  • OATH secrets
  • OTP slot secrets
  • OpenPGP private keys
  • PINs and role credentials
  • HSM keys and DKEK material

docs.title: Host attacker
docs.text:
Everything arriving over USB should be treated as attacker-controlled if the host is compromised.

Defenses include:

  • PIN or user verification
  • physical confirmation
  • OpenPGP role separation
  • retry counters and lockouts
  • applet-specific management keys or policy gates

Even with those defenses:

  • a compromised host can request operations while the device is connected
  • if the user authorizes an operation, the device may perform it
  • touch confirms presence, not intent for every byte in the request

docs.title: Powered-off theft
docs.text:
At-rest protection depends heavily on hardware:

  • RP2040 is weaker
  • RP2350/RP2354 and ESP32-S3 class devices provide stronger primitives
  • OTP-backed sealing and secure boot are meaningful only after correct provisioning

Describe a device as hardened only when the required protections have been provisioned and verified on that hardware.

docs.title: Firmware replacement
docs.text:
Secure boot and lock mechanisms can prevent unauthorized firmware from running, but only when enabled correctly on hardware that supports them.

Anti-rollback is a separate concern. It prevents older signed firmware from being accepted after the owner raises the rollback floor.

docs.title: Physical attacks
docs.text:
Microcontroller boards are not secure elements.

Out of scope:

  • decapping
  • microprobing
  • advanced fault injection
  • power and EM side channels
  • invasive lab extraction

For threats involving a well-funded laboratory, use certified secure hardware.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
The firmware families documented here are USB-facing. There is no independent network stack in the device model.

Network exposure comes from the host or from services using the credentials, not from the device itself.

docs.title: Reporting and documentation discipline
docs.text:
When documenting a security claim, include:

  • the firmware family
  • the board family
  • the provisioning state
  • the host tool path used to verify it

Include all four details so readers can understand exactly what the claim covers.
